topic.subject: social
topic.title: The French Revolution
topic.scope: estates, storming of the Bastille, Declaration of Rights, Jacobins, Napoleon, ideas of liberty and equality

concepts.name: Social Structure of the Three Estates

misconceptions.statement: The Third Estate consisted only of poor peasants and landless laborers.
misconceptions.why: Students often equate the entire Third Estate with the poorest section of society due to the focus on the struggle of the common man.
misconceptions.fix: The Third Estate was diverse, including wealthy merchants, lawyers, and educated professionals alongside peasants and artisans.

probe.question: Who were the members of the Third Estate?
probe.wrong_answer: Only the poor farmers and workers who had no money.

misconceptions.statement: The French Revolution happened because the King was personally poor and had no money.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the state's financial crisis with the personal poverty of the monarch.
misconceptions.fix: The French state was in debt due to long wars and the cost of maintaining the royal court, not because the King was personally destitute.

probe.question: Why did the French government face a financial crisis?
probe.wrong_answer: Because King Louis XVI was a poor man who could not afford to run his palace.

concepts.name: The Storming of the Bastille and Political Unrest

misconceptions.statement: The Bastille was a massive military fort that protected the King from the people.
misconceptions.why: Students associate the term 'Bastille' with a grand military defensive structure rather than a symbol of royal despotism.
misconceptions.fix: The Bastille was a hated prison that symbolized the King's absolute power, and its fall represented the start of the revolution.

probe.question: Why did the people attack the Bastille?
probe.wrong_answer: To capture the King's main military base and stop his army from attacking them.

concepts.name: Declaration of Rights and Democratic Ideals

misconceptions.statement: The Declaration of Rights granted equal voting rights to all men and women in France immediately.
misconceptions.why: Students project modern democratic standards onto the 18th century, assuming 'rights' meant universal suffrage.
misconceptions.fix: The Declaration established rights for 'active citizens' (men over 25 who paid taxes), excluding women and poor men.

probe.question: Who was allowed to vote after the Declaration of Rights?
probe.wrong_answer: Every man and woman living in France.

concepts.name: Jacobins and the Reign of Terror

misconceptions.statement: The Jacobins were the only political group that wanted a Republic.
misconceptions.why: Textbooks focus heavily on the Jacobins, leading students to assume they were the sole representatives of republicanism.
misconceptions.fix: There were other political clubs and factions, but the Jacobins became the most radical and dominant group during the Reign of Terror.

probe.question: Were the Jacobins the only group fighting for a Republic?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they were the only people who wanted to end the monarchy.

concepts.name: Napoleon and the Legacy of the Revolution

misconceptions.statement: Napoleon was a democratic leader who was elected by the people to bring freedom.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse Napoleon's modernization of laws with the establishment of a democratic government.
misconceptions.fix: Napoleon was a military dictator who crowned himself Emperor, though he did introduce some revolutionary legal reforms.

probe.question: What kind of ruler was Napoleon?
probe.wrong_answer: He was a democratically elected president who brought liberty to France.
